title: People who cannot manage their thirst. Part 2
scripture_text: ‘’The Pharisees heard the crowd whispering such things about him. Then the Chief Priests and the Pharisees sent temple guards to arrest him. Jesus said “I am with you for only a short time and then I am going to the one who sent me. You will look for me, but you will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come.” The Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go that we cannot find him? Will he go where our people live scattered among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks? What did he mean when he said, ‘You will look for me, but you will not find me,’ and ‘Where I am, you cannot come’?”
devotional:
On the last and greatest day of the festival, Jesus stood and said in a loud voice, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from within them.” By this he meant the Spirit whom those who believed in him were later to receive. Up to that time the Spirit had not been given, since Jesus had not yet been glorified. On hearing his words, some of the people said, “Surely this man is the Prophet.” Others said, “He is the Messiah.” Still others asked, “How can the Messiah come from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that the Messiah will come from David’s descendants and from Bethlehem the town where David lived?” Thus the people were divided because of Jesus. Some wanted to seize him, but no one laid a hand on him. Finally the temple guards went back to the chief priests and the Pharisees, who asked them, “Why didn’t you bring him in?” “No one ever spoke the way this man does,” the guards replied. “You mean he has deceived you also?” the Pharisees retorted.“Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed in him? No! But this mob that knows nothing of the law—there is a curse on them.”

Trying to arrest Jesus.

As the Pharisees mingle with the crowd, they become aware of the widespread discussions taking place concerning Jesus. John informs us that ‘Many in the crowd put their trust in him.’

This causes the religious leaders to panic, so they take the initiative in acting against Jesus, persuading the priestly authorities, who were in charge of the temple, to have Jesus arrested. In some ways this is a crucial moment for the Pharisees. They had hoped that fear and intimidation would have silenced Jesus and would have dissuaded the crowds from listening to him. But that had not happened. So in a doomed attempt to regain control, they decide to have Jesus arrested.

Sometimes when people feel threatened they can become aggressive. Their aggression is really an expression of perverted thirst for power, prestige and control.

I have often seen people act this way when someone else is calling the shots or takes the limelight away from them. Their sense of powerlessness leads them to become aggressive, tense, defensive and even angry, wanting to silence the other person.

We all develop subtle ways of trying to silence those who threaten our identity and make us feel vulnerable. Sometimes we question or ‘correct’ every statement they make or try to finish their sentences – as if to say “I think what she really means to say is…” At other times we ‘talk over them’, literally forcing our words to ride roughshod over theirs. Or we simple use a disparaging tone or sarcasm to belittle or embarrass them.

As the religious leaders listened to Jesus and saw the effect he had on the crowds, they made a desperate attempt to try and silence him in order to protect their perverted thirst for power and control. So they sent the temple guards to arrest him.

The Greek word for guards is huperetes, which means “servants.” It literally means an ‘under-rower’. In ancient days, it referred to those slaves who rowed the sailing ships below deck. These guards were at the disposal of the Sanhedrin, having various duties, “half cultic officials and half police” [Bultmann, p306]. They were considered as the lowest of the low, and the Pharisees sent them to arrest Jesus. At this time, because of the response of some of the people, these religious leaders were too afraid to come to Jesus themselves. So instead, they sent others who they think are dispensable to do their dirty work for them. If the crowds began to riot, they wouldn’t be caught in the middle.

This again is a sinful ploy that we are all guilty of using. Our vulnerability can often prevent us from dealing with an issue ourselves; we don’t want to lose face, so we use others to do our dirty work for us.

The temple guards had come to arrest Jesus, but instead he ‘arrests’ them.

As they listened to Jesus, they sensed something in the air, something majestic, something powerful, something different. So rather than following through with their assignment, they linger with the crowd and listen in. Instead of taking Jesus captive, these men find themselves being captivated by his life-giving words. Later on in the chapter John writes ‘Finally the temple guards went back to the chief priests and Pharisees who asked them. Why didn’t you bring him in?’ ‘No one ever spoke the way this man does, the guards declared.’ (vv45-46)

It appears that to some degree these soldiers had understood Jesus’ teaching and were able to withstand the pressure to arrest an innocent man who spoke authoritative truth.

So what did these guards hear that prevented them from arresting Jesus?

They heard someone speak with a sense of hope despite being in very difficult circumstances.

Look at what Jesus says. ‘I am with you for only a short time, and then I go to the one who sent me.’ John 7:33.

Jesus seemed to have an acute awareness that what he suffered and experienced in this life would not last for ever, because one day he would return to his Father. Despite his many trials and his profound suffering, Jesus had a sense of hope about the future.

Let me share the following story online:

Bible.org/illustrations/laboratory-experiment.

‘’A number of years ago researchers performed an experiment to see the effect hope has on those undergoing hardship. Two sets of laboratory rats were placed in separate tubs of water. The researchers left one set in the water and found that within an hour they had all drowned. The other rats were periodically lifted out of the water and then returned. When that happened, the second set of rats swam for over 24 hours. Why? Not because they were given a rest, but because they suddenly had hope! Those animals somehow hoped that if they could stay afloat just a little longer, someone would reach down and rescue them. If hope holds such power for unthinking rodents, how much greater should is effect be on our lives.’’ Today in the Word, May, 1990, MBI, p. 34

Hope is essential if we are going to cope with the pressures and demands of life. Hope is something that others find irresistible, it gives a person the ability to live and speak with authority and confidence. Hope is much more than a concept or a theory – it’s something that needs to live in our hearts, given us a healthy perspective on our present reality. Hope has to be experienced not explained.

On the other hand, hopelessness is the belief that this world gives us all we need for life and this is as good as it gets. Hopelessness can be an evidence of unsatisfied thirst, robbing a person of confidence and courage. Emil Bruner said "What oxygen is to the lungs, such is hope to the meaning of life."

They heard someone 'speak with boldness.’

Jesus knew that his time had not yet come; he had a certainty that no one could touch him or stop him until the Father allowed it to happen. This gives him the freedom to be courageous. He had nothing to hide, so he lets people know what is going to happen: "I am going to be with you just a little while longer and then I will go away to him who sent me. You will seek for me but you will not find me." John 7:33-34.

Jesus didn’t allow himself to be threatened by the evil plots of men. He wasn’t fearful, He was in control.

We need to have a strong sense of destiny that is rooted in the belief that our lives belong to a sovereign God who is in absolute control, and who will not allow anything to happen to us outside His will. Grasping the truth of God’s sovereign control will empower us, giving us both authority and confidence.
prayer: Father may I be nourished and comforted by the truth that you are the sovereign God.
